title: Identifiability of Child's Location Data
description: Live GPS coordinates transmitted from child's device to backend are inherently identifiable to the specific child, enabling precise location tracking and profiling.
assumptions: GPS data is transmitted with sufficient precision to identify individual location

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Location Data
description: Live GPS coordinates could be disclosed to unauthorized third parties through backend compromise, data breaches, or improper access controls.
assumptions: Backend system may have inadequate access controls or security measures

title: Excessive Data Collection via Continuous GPS Tracking
description: Regular interval transmission of live GPS coordinates may exceed data minimization principles if the stated purpose does not require continuous location monitoring.
assumptions: Purpose of data collection does not justify continuous live tracking

title: Unauthorized Use of Location Data for Secondary Purposes
description: Backend process may use collected GPS coordinates for purposes beyond the original intent (e.g., marketing, profiling, sharing with third parties).
assumptions: Backend may have capabilities to repurpose location data without explicit consent

title: Unnecessary Location Data Collection
description: The backend writes location pings to the Location History Store. If the system collects more location data than strictly required for its intended purpose (e.g., navigation, tracking), this violates the minimality principle. Explicit disclosure of personal location data may be avoidable if the system could function with less granular or less frequent location data.
assumptions: Location data is personal data; the system's purpose is known; minimality principle applies
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 from context [5] as it describes data disclosure across boundaries. The exact tree node may vary based on full LINDDUN Pro methodology.

title: Location Data Linkability
description: Location history data can be linked to identify specific individuals and their movements over time. Even if anonymized, patterns in location data can potentially be re-identified when combined with other data sources.
assumptions: Location data is inherently linkable to individuals; linkage attacks are possible
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a reasonable node for linkability threats in LINDDUN Pro.

title: Location Data Identifiability
description: Location pings can directly identify individuals and their whereabouts. The data store contains personal information that can be used to identify specific users without additional identifiers.
assumptions: Location data is personally identifiable information; the data store is accessible to authorized parties
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable node for identifiability threats in LINDDUN Pro.

title: Unnecessary Location Data Transfer to Geofencing Engine
description: The Mobile App Backend forwards location pings to the Geofencing Engine, potentially transferring more personal location data than strictly necessary for zone entry/exit detection. This explicit disclosure may violate the minimality principle if the geofencing engine could operate with less granular or aggregated location information.
assumptions: Location data is considered personal data; the transfer is not fully minimized to what's required for geofencing functionality.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] about data disclosure; the exact tree node may vary in LINDDUN Pro implementation.

title: Geofencing Engine Receives Personal Location Data Without Clear Purpose Limitation
description: The Geofencing & Alert Engine receives location pings from the backend, creating a data disclosure boundary. If the engine's purpose extends beyond zone detection (e.g., storing, analyzing, or sharing location data), this could constitute avoidable disclosure of personal data.
assumptions: The geofencing engine may have additional functions beyond the stated zone entry/exit checking; data minimality is not guaranteed.
uncertainty_note: Context [5] supports Dd for data disclosure across boundaries; exact tree node may vary.

title: Location Data Can Be Used to Identify or Track Individuals
description: Location pings forwarded from the backend to the geofencing engine contain personal data that can be used to identify or track individuals' movements, potentially enabling profiling or surveillance beyond the intended geofencing purpose.
assumptions: Location data is personally identifiable; the system may not have adequate anonymization or pseudonymization.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable node for identification threats; context [3] confirms I is applicable for Process→Process flows.

title: Linkability of Zone Definitions to Other Data Flows
description: Zone definitions (home, school, friend's house) stored in DS2 could be linked with other data flows (e.g., family member profiles, device locations, activity logs) to create comprehensive behavioral profiles of family members, potentially revealing patterns of movement and associations.
assumptions: Other data flows exist that contain complementary information about family members

title: Identification of Family Members' Locations
description: Zone definitions stored in DS2 could reveal sensitive location information about family members (e.g., home address, school location, friend's house), potentially enabling identification of individuals or their whereabouts even without explicit personal identifiers.
assumptions: Zone definitions contain identifiable location data that could be inferred or directly observed

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Zone Definitions
description: Zone definitions in DS2 could be accessed by unauthorized parties through vulnerabilities in the data store, improper access controls, or through the Geofencing Engine (P2) if it leaks data during processing, exposing private location information.
assumptions: Access controls on DS2 or P2 are not properly implemented or are bypassed

title: Linkability During Geofencing Processing
description: The Geofencing Engine (P2) could link zone definitions from DS2 with real-time location data from other sources (e.g., device GPS, user activity) to track family members' movements across multiple contexts, creating detailed surveillance profiles.
assumptions: P2 has access to or can correlate with other location data sources

title: Data Degradation During Geofencing Processing
description: Zone definitions could be corrupted, altered, or degraded during processing in P2, leading to incorrect geofencing behavior, false alerts, or loss of accurate location-based privacy controls.
assumptions: P2 has data processing vulnerabilities or lacks proper data integrity checks

title: Linkability of Geofencing Notifications
description: Arrival/departure notifications from the Geofencing Engine could be linked across multiple events to reconstruct detailed movement patterns of the child, potentially revealing sensitive information about routines, locations, and activities.
assumptions: Notifications are transmitted in a way that allows correlation across time and events
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a general linkability node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary based on full threat tree

title: Identification of Child's Location and Movements
description: The geofencing notifications inherently identify the child's location and movement patterns, which could be used to track the child's whereabouts and potentially infer sensitive information about their daily activities and habits.
assumptions: Notifications contain or can be correlated with child identity information
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a general identification node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary based on full threat tree

title: Disclosure of Geofencing Notifications to Unauthorized Parties
description: Arrival/departure notifications could be disclosed to unauthorized parties through interception, logging, or improper access controls, exposing the child's location and movement data to entities without legitimate need to know.
assumptions: Notifications are transmitted over networks or stored in systems with potential access vulnerabilities
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a general disclosure node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary based on full threat tree

title: Usurpation of Geofencing Notification Functionality
description: An attacker could potentially impersonate the Geofencing Engine or manipulate notifications to send false arrival/departure alerts, which could be used to mislead the parent or other system components about the child's actual location.
assumptions: Notifications are not cryptographically signed or authenticated
uncertainty_note: Tree node U.1.1 is a general usurpation node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary based on full threat tree

title: Parent Identity Impersonation During Registration
description: An attacker could impersonate the parent to register an account and create a false child profile, potentially leading to unauthorized access to child data or creation of fraudulent profiles.
assumptions: The registration process lacks robust identity verification mechanisms.
uncertainty_note: Tree node U.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro usurpation node for external entity flows.

title: False Child Profile Information
description: The parent could provide false or misleading information about the child (name, DOB, school) during profile creation, which could lead to incorrect data processing and potential privacy violations.
assumptions: No validation or verification of the provided child information.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro data deception node.

title: Unauthorized Child Profile Disclosure
description: The mobile app backend could disclose the child's sensitive profile information (name, DOB, school, geofence zones) to unauthorized parties or through insecure data transmission.
assumptions: Inadequate access controls and encryption for child profile data.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro disclosure node for process flows.

title: Parent-Child Profile Linkability
description: The system could link the parent's identity with the child's profile data, potentially exposing the child's information through the parent's account or enabling tracking of the child's activities across different contexts.
assumptions: The system stores and processes both parent and child data in a way that enables correlation.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro linkability node.

title: Child Identification Through Parent Registration
description: The child could be indirectly identified through the parent's registration data, as the child's profile (name, DOB, school) is created during the parent's account registration process.
assumptions: Child information is stored in association with parent account without proper anonymization.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a standard LINDDUN Pro identification node.

title: Excessive Personal Data Storage in Family Account Store
description: The backend stores comprehensive account, child profile, and geofence zone data. This raises concerns about data minimality - are all these data elements strictly necessary for the intended functionality? Implicit disclosure risks exist if stored data can be accessed by unauthorized parties or if the data collection scope exceeds what's required for the service.
assumptions: The system stores more personal data than minimally required for the stated functionality
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [3] about data disclosure and minimality principle

title: Child Profile Data Identifiability Risk

assumptions: Child profile data contains sufficient PII to identify individuals
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 chosen based on standard LINDDUN Pro identifiability threat structure

title: Geofence Zone Data Integrity Risk
description: Geofence zone data stored in DS2 could be tampered with or corrupted, potentially leading to incorrect location-based services, false alerts, or security vulnerabilities. Data integrity is critical for location-based functionality.
assumptions: Stored geofence data could be modified by unauthorized actors
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 based on standard LINDDUN Pro data integrity threat structure

title: Linkability Across Stored Data Elements
description: Multiple data elements (account info, child profiles, geofence zones) stored together in DS2 could be linked to create comprehensive profiles of individuals and families. This linkability could enable inference attacks or unauthorized profiling.
assumptions: Multiple data elements can be correlated to identify individuals
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 based on standard LINDDUN Pro linkability threat structure

title: Excessive location data collection

assumptions: Data minimization principles may not be fully implemented
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 chosen based on general data minimization methodology; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Location History
description: Location history data stored in DS1 could be disclosed to unauthorized parties if access controls on the data store or the retrieval process are inadequate. This includes potential breaches through compromised backend systems, insider threats, or insufficient authentication/authorization mechanisms.
assumptions: Access controls are not properly implemented or enforced; the backend system may be vulnerable to unauthorized access.

title: Usurpation of Parent Identity for Location History Access
description: An attacker could potentially impersonate the parent user to access their location history data. This could occur through credential theft, session hijacking, or social engineering attacks targeting the parent's authentication.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms may be vulnerable to credential compromise; the system may not have proper identity verification for sensitive data access.

title: Identification Through Location History Data
description: Location history data can be used to identify the parent's identity, movements, routines, and potentially their home/work locations. This data is inherently identifying and can reveal sensitive personal information about the user's daily life.
assumptions: Location data contains sufficient granularity to identify individuals; the data may be combined with other information to enhance identification.

title: Linkability of Location History to Other Data
description: Location history data can be linked with other data sources (e.g., device identifiers, timestamps, app usage patterns) to create comprehensive user profiles. This enables tracking of user behavior across different contexts and services.
assumptions: Location data can be correlated with other data sources; the system may not have proper data anonymization or separation mechanisms.

title: Parent Identity Linked to Child Location Data
description: When the parent (EE1) initiates the invitation to share child's location with a secondary guardian, the parent's identity becomes linked to the child's location data. This creates a privacy risk where the parent's association with the child's movements is exposed.
assumptions: The system logs or transmits metadata linking parent identity to location sharing events
uncertainty_note: Using generic LINDDUN Pro node L.1.1 as specific tree node not provided in context

title: Child Location Data Disclosed to Secondary Guardian
description: The mobile app backend (P1) transmits child's location data to the secondary guardian. This disclosure could expose sensitive location information to parties who may not have full authorization or understanding of privacy implications.
assumptions: Secondary guardian access is granted but may not be strictly limited to necessary data
uncertainty_note: Using generic LINDDUN Pro node D.1.1 as specific tree node not provided in context

title: Child Identity Inferred from Location Patterns
description: The mobile app backend (P1) processes location data that could reveal the child's identity through location patterns, routines, or associated metadata. Even if the child's name isn't directly transmitted, patterns could enable identification.
assumptions: Location data includes metadata or patterns that could enable identification
uncertainty_note: Using generic LINDDUN Pro node I.1.1 as specific tree node not provided in context

title: Unauthorized Access to Location Sharing Functionality
description: The mobile app backend (P1) could be vulnerable to unauthorized access where someone impersonates the parent or secondary guardian to gain access to child's location data. This usurpation threat applies to the process handling the location sharing.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms may have vulnerabilities or social engineering risks
uncertainty_note: Using generic LINDDUN Pro node U.1.1 as specific tree node not provided in context

title: Linkability of child's location data to other personal information
description: The live location data shared with the secondary guardian could be linked to other personal information about the child (e.g., identity, schedule, activities), potentially revealing patterns of behavior or sensitive information about the child's whereabouts.
assumptions: The secondary guardian or third parties could correlate location data with other available information about the child.

title: Identifiability of child through location tracking
description: Live location data can potentially identify the child's identity, especially if the guardian or unauthorized third parties can track movements and infer the child's identity from location patterns or shared context.
assumptions: Location data combined with other context (time, location names, etc.) could reveal the child's identity to unauthorized parties.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of child's location to third parties
description: The live location data shared with the secondary guardian could be further disclosed to unauthorized third parties (e.g., other family members, malicious actors, or the guardian could share it beyond intended scope).
assumptions: The secondary guardian may not be trusted to keep the location data confidential, or the data could be intercepted during transmission.

title: Usurpation of child's location data by unauthorized parties
description: Unauthorized parties could potentially impersonate the secondary guardian or the child to access or manipulate the location data, leading to stalking, harassment, or other harmful activities.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms may be insufficient to prevent unauthorized access to the location data stream.

title: Analytics data disclosure to unauthorized third parties
description: Advertising/analytics partner may share or sell the aggregated usage data to additional third parties beyond the intended scope, potentially exposing user behavior patterns to entities without proper consent or legal basis.
assumptions: Partner has business incentives to monetize data beyond the agreed scope; data may be re-identifiable when combined with other datasets
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a general disclosure node; specific partner contract terms would determine exact risk level

title: Regulatory non-compliance in data sharing
description: Sharing aggregated analytics with external advertising partner may violate GDPR, CCPA, or other privacy regulations if data is not properly anonymized, if consent was not obtained, or if data minimization principles are not followed.
assumptions: User consent mechanisms may not cover third-party analytics sharing; data may contain quasi-identifiers that enable re-identification
uncertainty_note: Specific regulatory requirements depend on jurisdiction and exact data content; 'aggregated' claim needs verification

title: Linkability of aggregated data across datasets
description: Even aggregated analytics data may be linkable when combined with other datasets held by the partner or other entities, potentially enabling user profiling or re-identification through statistical correlation.
assumptions: Partner has access to other datasets; statistical techniques can de-anonymize aggregated data under certain conditions
uncertainty_note: Risk depends on granularity of aggregation and partner's data ecosystem; 'aggregated' claim needs technical verification
